tool.name: curl
tool.tagline: Command-line tool for making HTTP and other URL requests
tool.description: curl transfers data to and from URLs from the command line, supporting HTTP(S) and dozens of other protocols. Developers use it to test and debug APIs, download files, script integrations and reproduce requests exactly, and its library libcurl powers networking in countless applications and devices.

glossary.def: A small program you run in a terminal to send a request to a web address and print the reply, e.g. curl https://example.com.
One Name: value line of extra information at the top of an HTTP request or response, such as Content-Type: text/html.
The small live table curl prints while downloading, showing how much has arrived, how fast and how long is left. -s hides it.
The HTTP method that asks for a response's headers only, without the body, e.g. to check a file's size before downloading it.
A body format that sends each form field as its own separate part, so whole files can be uploaded alongside text fields. curl -F builds it.
A separate terminal program for reading, filtering and building JSON data, often used together with curl.
Time to first byte: how long after starting a request the first byte of the response arrives.
A text file where curl saves cookies (with -c) and reads them back (with -b), so several commands can share one signed-in session.
A unique ID a client sends with a request so that, if it tries again, the server recognises the repeat and doesn't do the work twice.
A file listing the certificate authorities a program trusts; curl checks every server certificate against it.
A site's certificate plus the certificates that signed it, leading back to an authority the device already trusts.
The common text format for certificate and key files: base64-looking text between lines like -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----.
The encryption method a TLS connection uses, agreed by both sides during the handshake, e.g. TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384.
TLS where the client also shows a certificate, so the server can check who is connecting, not just the other way round.
The secret half of a key pair that only its owner keeps; it proves the owner's identity and must never be shared.
The host name a client announces at the very start of TLS, so a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to show.
curl's own patterns inside a URL, like [1-10] or {a,b}, that stand for many URLs fetched in one command.
Part of setting up TLS where client and server agree which protocol to speak next, such as HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1.
A newer way to carry internet connections, built on UDP, with encryption built in and independent streams; HTTP/3 runs on it.
A response header in which a server says it is also reachable another way, such as over HTTP/3, so clients can switch next time.
Carrying many separate conversations over one connection at the same time, their pieces interleaved.
When one slow or lost item at the front of a queue holds up everything behind it, like one slow shopper at a single checkout.
A listing of raw data with every byte written as a two-digit code (hexadecimal), so you can see exactly what was sent.
A simple kind of proxy that just relays network connections without understanding what's inside them.
An old way for a web server to answer a request by running a separate script, passing request details in environment variables.
Turning a host name like example.com into the numeric IP address a computer connects to, usually by asking DNS.
Sending DNS lookups as encrypted HTTPS requests, so others on the network can't see or change which names you look up.
The library behind the curl command: ready-made C code that other programs and languages build in to make transfers.
libcurl's simple way of making one transfer at a time: create a handle, set options, run it, clean up.
libcurl's way of running many transfers at the same time from one thread, checking repeatedly which can move forward.

concepts.name: How the web talks: requests and responses
concepts.summary: A client sends a request to a URL; a server sends back a response with a status code, headers and a body. curl lets you see all of it.
concepts.why: Every curl command is one of these conversations, so knowing their parts makes every option that follows make sense.
concepts.body:
When you open a website, your computer sends a short message to another computer on the internet and gets a reply. The computer that asks is the **client**. The one that answers is the **server**: a computer that stays switched on, waiting for questions, like a shop counter waiting for customers.

Usually the client is your **browser** (Chrome, Safari, Firefox), which turns the reply into a page you can look at. **curl** is a client you run in the terminal. It sends the same kind of message but simply prints the reply as text, so you see exactly what the server said.

Every message is aimed at a **URL**, the address you type into a browser. In `https://api.example.com/users?limit=5`, `https://` says how to talk, `api.example.com` names the server and `/users` the thing you want on it. The part after `?` is the **query string**: extra settings as `name=value` pairs, joined by `&`.

The rules for these messages are called **HTTP**. A set of rules both sides agree to follow, so they understand each other, is called a **protocol**: like the fixed layout of a letter, with the address in one place and the signature in another.

**HTTPS** is HTTP sent through a locked, scrambled connection, so nobody between you and the server can read or change it. The locking layer is called **TLS**. Almost every site uses HTTPS today; you just write `https://` and curl handles the rest.

The client's message is the **request**. Its first word is the **HTTP method**, a verb saying what you want: **GET** means "send me this", **POST** means "here is some data for you". GET is what curl sends unless you ask for something else.

After that line come **headers**: one `Name: value` line each, with extra details such as which formats the client accepts. A request can also carry a **body**, the data being sent, such as what you typed into a form.

The server's reply is the **response**. It starts with a **status code**, a three-digit number saying how it went: `200` means OK, `404` means "not found", `500` means the server itself failed. Then come response headers, such as `Content-Type: text/html` ("what follows is a web page"), and then the body: the page, picture or data you asked for.
concepts.code:
curl https://example.com          # prints only the response body

# What curl sends for you (the request):
#   GET / HTTP/1.1                <- HTTP method, path, HTTP version
#   Host: example.com             <- headers, one per line
#   User-Agent: curl/8.16.0
#   Accept: */*
#
# What the server sends back (the response):
#   HTTP/1.1 200 OK               <- status code 200 = OK
#   Content-Type: text/html       <- response headers
#   Content-Length: 1256
#
#   <!doctype html> ...           <- the body: the page itself
takeaways: A client sends a request to a URL; the server answers with a response
Request = HTTP method (GET, POST...) + headers + optional body
Response = status code (200, 404, 500...) + headers + body
HTTPS is HTTP through a locked connection (TLS)
pitfalls: Expecting curl to show a page like a browser does: it prints the raw text the server sent, which for a web page is the code a browser would turn into the page.

quiz.q: In `https://shop.example.com/search?q=lamp&page=2`, which part is the query string?
quiz.explain: The query string is everything after the ?, here two name=value pairs joined by &.

quiz.q: A server answers with status code 404. What does that tell you?
options: The thing you asked for was not found
quiz.explain: 404 means "not found"; 200 means OK and codes in the 500s mean the server failed.

concepts.name: Your first requests: GET and downloads
concepts.summary: curl URL prints the body of the response; -o and -O save it to a file, -L follows redirects and -s hides the progress meter.
concepts.why: Fetching a URL from the terminal is the starting point for downloading files and for testing the services programs talk to.
concepts.body:
Give curl a URL and it sends a GET request and prints the response body. It prints it to standard output, so you can redirect it to a file or pipe it into another command like any other output. The status code and headers aren't shown unless you ask (next lesson).

Saving output:

- `-o file` saves the body to a file you name.
- `-O` (capital O) names the file after the last part of the URL: `curl -O https://example.com/app.tar.gz` saves `app.tar.gz`.
- `--output-dir dir` picks the folder to save into, and `-J` uses the file name the server suggests in a header instead.

When the body goes to a file or a pipe, curl draws a **progress meter** on standard error: a small live table of how much has arrived and how fast. `-s` (silent) hides it. `-sS` hides it but still prints error messages, which is the usual choice in scripts.

Sometimes a server answers "it's not here, go to this other URL instead". That's a **redirect**: a status code in the 300s plus a `Location` header holding the new address. curl doesn't follow redirects by default, so you get that short "moved" reply instead of the file. Add `-L` to follow them; downloads from GitHub and many other sites need it.

Quote URLs that contain `&`, `?` or `[`. Otherwise the shell treats those characters specially before curl ever sees them; an unquoted `&`, for example, cuts the URL short. So write `curl 'https://api.example.com/search?q=cat&limit=5'`.

`curl --version` shows which version you have and which features it supports.
concepts.code:
curl https://example.com                      # body to standard output
curl -sS -o page.html https://example.com     # save it; quiet, but show errors
curl -LO https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-1.7.1/jq-linux-amd64
curl -L -o jq --output-dir ~/bin https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-1.7.1/jq-linux-amd64
curl 'https://api.example.com/search?q=cat&limit=5'   # quote the URL!
curl -sS https://api.github.com/repos/curl/curl | head -5
curl --version | head -1                      # curl 8.x (...) libcurl/8.x OpenSSL/3...
takeaways: curl URL = a GET request, body to standard output
-o name saves under your name, -O under the URL's; -L follows redirects
-sS: no progress meter, but errors still show
pitfalls: Forgetting -L and saving a tiny "moved" reply instead of the file.

quiz.q: `curl -O https://dl.example.com/latest` saved a 150-byte file instead of the 20 MB release. Most likely fix?
quiz.explain: The URL answered with a redirect, which curl does not follow unless -L is given.

concepts.name: Seeing headers: -i, -I, -v and -H
concepts.summary: Show response headers with -i, ask for headers only with -I, watch the whole exchange with -v and add your own request headers with -H.
concepts.why: Many problems, such as the wrong format or a missing login, show up only in headers, so seeing and setting them is essential.
concepts.body:
A response has three parts: the status line (with the status code), the headers, and the body. curl prints only the body unless you ask for more:

- `-i` includes the status line and headers before the body.
- `-I` sends a **HEAD** request: an HTTP method that asks for the headers only, with no body. Handy for checking the status, `Content-Type` (what kind of data it is, such as `text/html` or `image/png`) or `Content-Length` (its size) of a big file without downloading it.

`-v` (verbose) shows the whole conversation. Lines starting with `>` are the request curl sent, lines starting with `<` are the response headers, and lines starting with `*` are curl's own notes on what it's doing. This extra output goes to standard error, so you can still pipe or save the body.

To send your own headers, use `-H 'Name: value'`, as many times as you need. curl adds a few by itself, such as `User-Agent: curl/8.x` (which program is asking) and `Accept: */*` (any format is fine). Your `-H` replaces curl's version of the same header, and an empty value removes it: `-H 'Accept:'`. `-A` is a shortcut for the User-Agent.

The `*` lines follow the steps of connecting, in order:

- curl looks up the server's name to find its numeric address, the way your phone looks up a contact's number. That lookup system is called **DNS**.
- It opens a connection to that address.
- For HTTPS, it sets up TLS and checks the server's **certificate**: a digital ID card, signed by an organisation everyone trusts, proving the server really is `example.com`.
- Then it sends the request and reads the response.

When a site "works in the browser but not with curl", compare the headers. Browsers have built-in developer tools that can copy any request as a ready-made curl command ("Copy as cURL"), so you can see exactly what the browser sent.

One catch: `-I` really sends HEAD, and some servers answer HEAD differently from GET. To see the headers of a real GET, use `-i`, or `-s -D - -o /dev/null` (`-D -` writes the headers to standard output and `-o /dev/null` throws the body away).
concepts.code:
curl -i https://example.com          # HTTP/2 200 + headers + body
curl -I https://example.com/big.iso  # HEAD: headers only
curl -v https://api.example.com/health
# * Connected to api.example.com (203.0.113.7) port 443    <- curl's notes
# > GET /health HTTP/2                                     <- what curl sent
# > User-Agent: curl/8.16.0
# < HTTP/2 200                                             <- what came back
# < content-type: application/json
curl -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'X-Request-Id: abc123' https://api.example.com/items
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null https://example.com   # GET, print only the headers
takeaways: -i adds response headers, -I sends HEAD, -v shows the whole exchange
-H 'Name: value' sets a request header; -H 'Name:' removes one
In -v output: * curl's notes, > sent, < received
pitfalls: Using -I to check a URL whose server answers HEAD differently from GET.

quiz.q: In `curl -v` output, what do lines starting with `>` show?
options: Headers curl sent in the request
quiz.explain: > marks data sent by curl, < marks data received, * is curl's own commentary.

concepts.name: POST, PUT and forms: -d, -X, -F
concepts.summary: Send form data with -d, pick another HTTP method with -X, upload files with -F, and encode awkward characters safely with --data-urlencode.
concepts.why: Creating or changing anything on a server means sending data in the request, and sending it in the right format avoids confusing errors.
concepts.body:
So far you've only asked for things. To send data, such as a sign-up form or a new item, you put it in the request body. `-d` (or `--data`) does that, and switches the request to POST automatically:

`curl -d 'name=Ann&age=30' https://example.com/users`

That body uses the same format a form on a web page sends when you press Submit: `name=value` pairs joined by `&`. curl labels it with the header `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, which tells the server "this is form data".

- `-d @file` reads the body from a file, but **removes its line breaks**. Use `--data-binary @file` to send a file exactly as it is.
- Several `-d` options are joined with `&`.

In this format `&` separates pairs and `=` separates a name from its value, so a value containing them would be misread. **URL encoding** solves that by replacing such characters with codes: a space becomes `+` or `%20`, `&` becomes `%26`. `--data-urlencode 'q=a b&c'` does it for you and sends `q=a+b%26c`. Use it for anything a person typed.

`-F` sends a different body format, **multipart**, which is what a page with a file-upload button uses: each field travels as its own part, so whole files fit. `-F 'title=Report' -F 'file=@report.pdf'` sends a text field and attaches a file. Add `;type=application/pdf` to label the file's kind of data.

Besides GET and POST, there are other HTTP methods for other jobs: **PUT** replaces something, **PATCH** changes part of it, **DELETE** removes it. `-X` sets the HTTP method: `-X PUT -d ...`, `-X DELETE`. It only changes that one word in the request; the body still comes from `-d`.

You don't need `-X POST` with `-d`, which is already POST. Avoid `-X` together with `-L`: curl would keep that HTTP method after every redirect, which is usually wrong. And never use `-X HEAD`; use `-I`.

`-G` moves the `-d` data into the URL's query string and sends a GET instead, handy for search pages: `curl -G --data-urlencode 'q=rust lang' https://api.example.com/search`.
concepts.code:
curl -d 'name=Ann&age=30' https://api.example.com/form
# body: name=Ann&age=30   Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
curl --data-urlencode 'q=a b&c' https://api.example.com/s
# body: q=a+b%26c
curl --data-binary @payload.xml -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' https://api.example.com/import
curl -F 'title=Q3 report' -F 'file=@report.pdf;type=application/pdf' https://api.example.com/upload
curl -X PUT -d 'status=done' https://api.example.com/tasks/7
curl -X DELETE https://api.example.com/tasks/7
curl -G --data-urlencode 'q=rust lang' https://api.example.com/search   # GET ?q=rust+lang
takeaways: -d sends form data as a POST; --data-binary @file sends a file unchanged
-F makes multipart uploads; @file attaches a file
-X only changes the HTTP method; -G moves -d data into the query string
pitfalls: Sending a file with -d @file when it must arrive unchanged: line breaks are removed. Use --data-binary @file.

quiz.q: What is sent by `curl -X PUT -d 'a=1' URL`?
options: A PUT with an empty body
quiz.explain: -X changes the method to PUT while -d still supplies the body.

quiz.q: Which option uploads a file the way a web page's upload button does?
quiz.explain: -F builds a multipart body, and @ attaches the file as one of its parts.

concepts.name: JSON APIs and authentication
concepts.summary: Call JSON APIs with --json, prove who you are with an access token or a username and password, and pipe the replies into jq.
concepts.why: Most services that programs talk to exchange JSON and want an access token, so this is everyday curl work.
concepts.body:
Many servers aren't built for people to look at but for programs to use. Such a server offers an **API**: a set of URLs a program can call to read or change data, like a weather service or a shop's product list. Because they work over HTTP, these are called web APIs, and they answer with data instead of pages.

That data is usually **JSON**, a text format for structured data that people can read too. `{"name": "Ann", "tags": ["admin", "ops"]}` describes something with a name and a list of two tags: curly braces hold `"key": value` pairs, square brackets hold lists.

To send JSON, use `--json` (curl 7.82+). It puts the data in the body, sends a POST, and sets two headers: `Content-Type: application/json` ("this body is JSON") and `Accept: application/json` ("please answer in JSON"):

`curl --json '{"name":"Ann"}' https://api.example.com/users`

`--json @user.json` reads a file and `--json @-` reads standard input, so you can pipe JSON in. Add `-X PATCH` or `-X PUT` for other HTTP methods. Older curl needs `-H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{...}'` instead.

Typing JSON inside shell quotes gets messy: a quote or line break in a value breaks it. **jq**, a separate terminal program for JSON with its own course, builds it safely: `jq -n --arg name "$NAME" '{name: $name}'` prints correct JSON whatever `$NAME` holds. Pipe that into `curl --json @-`.

Most APIs want to know who's calling. Proving who you are is called **authentication**. The common ways:

- An **access token**: a long secret string the service gave you, sent in a header on every request: `-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"`.
- An **API key**: the same idea, often sent in a custom header such as `-H "X-API-Key: $KEY"`.
- A username and password: `-u user:password`. `-u user` alone makes curl ask for the password, so it never appears in the command.

Don't type a token itself into a command: your shell saves typed commands in its history. Keep it in an environment variable and write `$TOKEN`. Finally, pipe the reply into jq to pick out what you need: `curl -sS ... | jq '.items[].name'` prints the name of every item.
concepts.code:
curl --json '{"name":"Ann","role":"admin"}' https://api.example.com/users
# sends a POST with Content-Type and Accept set to application/json
jq -n --arg name "$NAME" '{name: $name}' | curl --json @- https://api.example.com/users
curl -X PATCH --json '{"role":"viewer"}' https://api.example.com/users/42
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" https://api.example.com/me | jq .email
curl -u ann https://intranet.example.com/report     # asks for the password
curl -sS -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" 'https://api.example.com/items?limit=2' | jq '.items[].name'
takeaways: --json sets the body, Content-Type and Accept in one option
Token: `-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"`; username and password: `-u user`
Build JSON with jq and pipe it to --json @-
pitfalls: Pasting shell variables into hand-written JSON; a quote or line break in the value breaks the body.

quiz.q: What does `--json '{}'` set that a plain `-d '{}'` does not?
options: Content-Type and Accept headers for JSON
quiz.explain: -d already makes a POST but uses a form Content-Type; --json sets both JSON headers.

concepts.name: Failing properly: --fail and exit codes
concepts.summary: By default curl exits 0 even when the server answers 404 or 500; use --fail or --fail-with-body and check exit codes in scripts.
concepts.why: Scripts that treat an error page as success silently pass on broken data; correct failure handling prevents that.
concepts.body:
A surprise for many: curl counts an HTTP error response as a **successful transfer**. `curl https://api.example.com/missing` returns exit code **0** while printing the 404 body. curl did its job; it's the server that said no.

To make HTTP errors fail:

- `-f` / `--fail` makes curl exit with code **22** for status 400 and above, and hides the body.
- `--fail-with-body` (7.76+) also exits 22 but still prints the body, which usually holds the server's explanation of what went wrong. Prefer it in scripts.

Other exit codes worth recognising:

- **6**: couldn't look up the host name (DNS failed).
- **7**: couldn't connect. Nothing is listening there, or a **firewall**, a network filter that blocks some connections, is in the way.
- **28**: a **timeout**, curl gave up waiting. **35**: setting up TLS failed. **60**: the server's certificate couldn't be verified.
- **56**: the connection broke while receiving data.

`man curl` lists them all under EXIT CODES, and with `-sS` curl prints a one-line explanation such as `curl: (7) Failed to connect...`.

In a script, put `set -euo pipefail` near the top. It makes bash stop at the first failing command (`-e`), treat unset variables as errors (`-u`) and count a failure anywhere in a pipeline (`pipefail`). Then `curl -sS --fail-with-body ...` stops the script with a readable error. Without `pipefail`, `curl ... | jq` reports only jq's exit status and hides curl's failure.

When you'd rather branch on the status than stop, capture it with `-w '%{http_code}'`, covered next.
concepts.code:
curl -s https://api.example.com/missing; echo "exit $?"
# {"error":"not found"}  exit 0      <- looks like success!
curl -sf https://api.example.com/missing; echo "exit $?"
# exit 22                            (no body)
curl -sS --fail-with-body https://api.example.com/missing; echo "exit $?"
# {"error":"not found"}  exit 22
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:1/; echo "exit $?"
# curl: (7) Failed to connect to 127.0.0.1 port 1 ... exit 7

set -euo pipefail
curl -sS --fail-with-body https://api.example.com/items | jq '.items | length'
takeaways: HTTP error statuses (400 and up) still exit 0 unless you pass --fail or --fail-with-body
Exit 6 DNS, 7 connect, 22 HTTP error, 28 timeout, 60 certificate
Use set -o pipefail when piping curl into other tools
pitfalls: Using -f in scripts and then wondering why the API's error message is missing; use --fail-with-body.

quiz.q: A script runs `curl -s URL > data.json` and the server answers 500. What is curl's exit code?
quiz.explain: Without --fail, an HTTP error response is still a completed transfer, so curl exits 0.

quiz.q: Which exit code means curl could not resolve the host name?
quiz.explain: Exit code 6 is 'Could not resolve host'; 7 is a failed connection.

concepts.name: Measuring with --write-out
concepts.summary: Print status codes, timings, sizes or a full JSON summary after a transfer with -w and its %{variables}.
concepts.why: Quick checks of the status and of where the time goes are invaluable when a service is slow or fails only some of the time.
concepts.body:
`-w` / `--write-out` prints a format string after the transfer, with `%{variable}` placeholders filled in. Combine it with `-o /dev/null -s` to print only what you ask for.

Common variables:

- `%{http_code}` the status code, `%{url_effective}` the final URL after redirects, `%{num_redirects}`.
- `%{size_download}`, `%{speed_download}`, `%{content_type}`, `%{http_version}`, `%{remote_ip}` (the numeric address curl connected to).

Timings are in seconds, each counted **from the start** of the request:

- `%{time_namelookup}`: the DNS lookup is done.
- `%{time_connect}`: the connection is open.
- `%{time_appconnect}`: TLS is set up.
- `%{time_starttransfer}`: the first byte of the response arrived, often called **TTFB** (time to first byte).
- `%{time_total}`: everything is done.

Because timings add up from the start, subtract neighbours to get each phase: TLS setup took `time_appconnect - time_connect`; the server's own thinking time is roughly `time_starttransfer - time_appconnect`.

Other handy forms: `-w '%{json}'` prints every variable as one JSON object (pipe it into jq), `%{header_json}` gives the response headers as JSON, `%header{content-type}` one single header, `-w @format.txt` reads the format from a file, and `%{stderr}` sends the rest of the output to standard error. `\n` in the format starts a new line.

A status check in one line: `code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "$URL")`. The `$( )` runs the command inside it and puts what it printed into the variable `code`; then branch on `$code`.
concepts.code:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com          # 200
curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective} after %{num_redirects}\n' http://github.com
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} tcp=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n' https://example.com
# dns=0.012 tcp=0.031 tls=0.068 ttfb=0.142 total=0.143
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{json}' https://example.com | jq '{http_code, time_total, http_version}'
code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://api.example.com/health)
[ "$code" = 200 ] || echo "unhealthy: $code"
takeaways: `-s -o /dev/null -w '...'` prints only the numbers you want
Timings count from the start; subtract neighbours to get each phase
-w '%{json}' prints every variable as JSON
pitfalls: Reading %{time_starttransfer} as the server's time alone; it also includes the DNS lookup and connection setup.

quiz.q: `time_connect` is 0.030 and `time_appconnect` is 0.095. What does 0.065 s represent?
quiz.explain: time_appconnect marks the end of TLS setup, which starts once the connection is open (time_connect).

concepts.name: Cookies and login sessions
concepts.summary: Websites remember a login with cookies: save them with -c, send them back with -b, and script logins that need them.
concepts.why: Testing websites and older services often means signing in once and reusing the cookie the sign-in gave you.
concepts.body:
Websites remember you with **cookies**: small pieces of data the server sends in a `Set-Cookie` response header. The browser stores them and sends them back in a `Cookie` header on every later request. After you sign in, one of them identifies your **session**, the server's record that you're signed in, so holding it is as good as holding your password.

curl ignores cookies unless you tell it otherwise. Two options cover almost everything:

- `-c jar.txt` (the "cookie jar") **writes** all cookies curl knows to a file when it finishes.
- `-b jar.txt` **reads** cookies from that file and sends the ones that match the URL. If the text after `-b` contains `=`, curl sends it as the cookie itself: `-b 'session=abc123'`.

Using both on the same file, `-b jar.txt -c jar.txt`, lets a series of commands behave like one browser visit: the sign-in response sets a session cookie, later requests send it, and any updated cookies are saved back.

A typical scripted sign-in:

- POST the username and password with `-c jar.txt`. Some login forms also contain a hidden one-time code you must send back; fetch the form first to read it.
- Call the pages that need you signed in with `-b jar.txt`.

The jar is a plain text file, one cookie per line with tab-separated fields (the old Netscape layout), so you can look inside. Expired cookies are dropped. Cookies with no expiry date, meant to last until the browser closes, are kept only because you save them. Passing `-b ''` (empty) switches cookie handling on without loading anything, which matters when you follow redirects with `-L` that set a cookie and then require it.

Treat jar files like passwords and delete them when you're done.
concepts.code:
# 1. sign in and save the session cookie
curl -sS -c jar.txt -d 'user=ann&password=hunter2' https://app.example.com/login
# 2. reuse it for requests that need you signed in
curl -sS -b jar.txt https://app.example.com/api/me
# {"user":"ann"}
# keep the jar updated across calls
curl -sS -b jar.txt -c jar.txt https://app.example.com/dashboard -o /dev/null
# send a cookie you already have instead of a file
curl -sS -b 'session=abc123; theme=dark' https://app.example.com/api/me
grep -v '^#' jar.txt      # fields: domain, path, secure, expiry, name, value
rm jar.txt
takeaways: -c file saves cookies, -b file sends them
-b 'name=value' sends that exact cookie
Use -b and -c on the same jar to act like one browser visit
pitfalls: Using -c only and expecting the next command to be logged in; reading requires -b.

quiz.q: Which pair of commands signs in and then calls a page that needs you signed in?
quiz.explain: -c writes the cookies from the login response; -b sends them on the next request.

concepts.name: Timeouts and retries
concepts.summary: Limit how long curl waits with --connect-timeout and --max-time, and retry temporary failures with --retry.
concepts.why: Without limits, a script can hang forever on a dead server; with retries, it survives brief outages.
concepts.body:
By default curl waits a long time: connecting gives up only after 300 seconds, and the whole transfer has **no** time limit. In scripts, and in health checks (small requests that just ask a service "are you up?"), always set limits:

- `--connect-timeout 5` limits opening the connection, TLS setup included.
- `-m 30` / `--max-time 30` limits the entire operation. Going over either gives exit code 28.

To **retry** is to try a failed request again automatically, because the problem may be brief:

- `--retry 3` retries up to three times when the error looks **temporary**: a timeout, or status 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504. The wait starts at 1 second and doubles each time, unless you set `--retry-delay`.
- For 429 ("too many requests") and 503 ("unavailable"), curl obeys the server's `Retry-After` header, which says how long to wait.
- `--retry-all-errors` retries on any error, including other HTTP errors when used with `--fail`; use it with care.
- `--retry-max-time 60` caps the total time spent retrying, and `--retry-connrefused` also retries when the connection is refused, useful while a service is still starting.

Be careful retrying requests that change things. A request is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once: reading a page, or setting a task's status to "done". Creating an order is not. If a POST timed out but actually succeeded, a retry creates a second order. Many APIs accept an `Idempotency-Key` header, a unique ID for each action, so the server can spot the repeat.

A good default for scripts: `curl -sS --fail-with-body --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 30 --retry 3`.
concepts.code:
curl -sS --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 https://api.example.com/report -o report.json
echo $?        # 28 if it took longer than 20 s

# robust download in an automated build
curl -fsSL --retry 5 --retry-delay 2 --retry-max-time 60 \
     -o tool.tgz https://releases.example.com/tool.tgz

# wait for a service that is still starting
curl -fsS --retry 10 --retry-connrefused --retry-delay 1 http://localhost:8080/health

# POST with an idempotency key so a retry cannot charge twice
# (uuidgen prints a new random ID each time)
curl -sS --retry 3 -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" --json @order.json https://api.example.com/orders
takeaways: --connect-timeout for connecting, --max-time for the whole request
--retry N handles timeouts and status 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504
Retrying requests that aren't idempotent can do the work twice
pitfalls: Running curl in a scheduled job or automated build without --max-time, so a stalled connection blocks it forever.

quiz.explain: curl treats those as temporary; --retry-all-errors widens it to everything.

concepts.name: TLS, certificates and host overrides
concepts.summary: Control certificate checks with --cacert, prove the client's identity with mutual TLS, and test a new server with --resolve and --connect-to.
concepts.why: Company-internal certificates, servers that check the client too, and testing a server before its name points at it are routine in real infrastructure.
concepts.body:
For `https://` URLs curl checks the server's certificate. Certificates are signed by a **certificate authority** (CA), an organisation that devices agree to trust. curl keeps its list of trusted CAs in a file called the **CA bundle**.

The check passes when the certificate was signed by a CA in that bundle, directly or through in-between certificates (together, the **certificate chain**), and its name matches the host name in the URL. A failed check gives exit code **60**; exit 35 means the **handshake**, the opening exchange that sets up TLS, failed.

- `--cacert internal-ca.pem` trusts an extra CA, such as your company's own. **PEM** is the usual text format for certificate files. `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` does the same through an environment variable.
- `-k` / `--insecure` turns checking off entirely. Fine for a one-off look at a test machine, never in scripts: anyone in between could pretend to be the server and read everything.
- `-v` shows the TLS version, the encryption recipe chosen (the **cipher**) and the certificate's subject (who it's for), issuer (who signed it) and expiry date, which usually explains a failure.

**Mutual TLS** (mTLS): the server also asks the client for a certificate, so both sides prove who they are. `--cert client.crt --key client.key` supplies the client's certificate and its **private key**, the secret half that only the owner holds, or one PEM file with both. Some services use this instead of tokens.

A server is reached at an **IP address**, the numeric address DNS looks up, and a **port**, a numbered door on that machine (443 for HTTPS). To test a new server before DNS sends its name there:

- `--resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.50` makes curl connect to that IP address for that name and port. The URL, the `Host` header and the **SNI** (the name curl announces at the start of TLS, so the server picks the right certificate) all still say `api.example.com`. Ideal for checking one server behind a **load balancer**, a front server that spreads requests over several copies.
- `--connect-to api.example.com:443:staging.internal:443` similarly sends the connection to another host name.

Don't fake the name with `-H 'Host: ...'` against an IP address over HTTPS: SNI and the certificate check would use the address, not the name.
concepts.code:
curl -sS https://intranet.corp/api            # curl: (60) SSL certificate problem
curl -sS --cacert corp-root-ca.pem https://intranet.corp/api   # OK
curl -sS --cert client.crt --key client.key https://mtls.example.com/v1/ping
curl -v https://example.com -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'SSL connection|subject|expire'
# * SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384   <- TLS version / cipher
# *  subject: CN=example.com
# *  expire date: Jan 15 23:59:59 2027 GMT
# test the new server before the DNS switch
curl -sS --resolve www.example.com:443:203.0.113.50 https://www.example.com/health
curl -sS --connect-to www.example.com:443:node-2.internal:443 https://www.example.com/
takeaways: --cacert trusts an extra CA; -k turns checking off (avoid)
--cert and --key for mutual TLS
--resolve and --connect-to reach a specific server under the real name
pitfalls: Adding -k to make an error go away in a script, leaving it permanently unverified.

quiz.q: You want to reach the new server at 203.0.113.50 as https://shop.example.com, with correct SNI and certificate checks, before DNS changes. Use:
quiz.explain: --resolve pins the address while keeping the URL's host name for SNI, Host and verification.

concepts.name: Config files and --variable
concepts.summary: Keep options and secrets out of your commands with -K config files, and fill values into headers and bodies with --variable and --expand-.
concepts.why: Long curl commands with tokens become reusable and safer once moved into config files and variables.
concepts.body:
Any command-line option can live in a **configuration file** (config file for short): a text file of settings, read with `-K file`, or `-K -` to read it from standard input. Each line is an option without its leading dashes, optionally with `=`: `header = "Authorization: Bearer xyz"`, `url = "https://..."`, `fail-with-body`. curl also reads `~/.curlrc` automatically unless the first option is `-q`.

Config files keep secrets such as passwords and tokens out of shell history and out of `ps`, which shows every running command with its arguments to anyone on the machine. They also let a team share request recipes. Feeding a config through standard input passes a header without it ever appearing in that process list:

`printf 'header = "Authorization: Bearer %s"\n' "$TOKEN" | curl -K - https://api.example.com/me`

**Variables** (curl 8.3+) let you write a command once as a **template**, with blanks like `{{name}}` that are filled in when it runs:

- `--variable name=value` sets one, `--variable name@file` loads a file's contents, and `--variable %NAME` copies in an environment variable (`%NAME=default` gives a fallback).
- Options starting with `--expand-` fill in the blanks: `--expand-header`, `--expand-url`, `--expand-data`, `--expand-json`...

Curl's **functions** change a value as it's filled in, and can be chained:

- `{{name:trim}}` removes spaces around it, `{{name:url}}` URL-encodes it.
- `{{name:json}}` adds backslashes before quotes and other special characters, so it's safe inside a JSON string (it doesn't add the surrounding quotes).
- `{{name:b64}}` converts it to **base64**, a way to write any data using only letters, digits and a few symbols.

Filling in only happens in `--expand-` options, so a `{{` anywhere else is sent exactly as written.
concepts.code:
# api.curl  -- a reusable request recipe
#   silent
#   show-error
#   fail-with-body
#   header = "Accept: application/json"
curl -K api.curl https://api.example.com/items

# pass a secret through standard input: never visible in ps
printf 'header = "Authorization: Bearer %s"\n' "$TOKEN" | curl -K - https://api.example.com/me

# variables (curl 8.3+)
curl --variable %TOKEN --expand-header 'Authorization: Bearer {{TOKEN}}' https://api.example.com/me
curl --variable 'q=rust & go' --expand-url 'https://api.example.com/search?q={{q:url}}'
curl --variable 'name=Ann "A"' --expand-json '{"name":"{{name:json}}"}' https://api.example.com/users
# body: {"name":"Ann \"A\""}
takeaways: -K file reads options from a file; ~/.curlrc is read automatically
--variable %ENV, name=value or name@file, filled in by --expand-* options
{{v:url}}, {{v:json}}, {{v:trim}} make values safe where they land
pitfalls: Putting tokens straight into commands on shared machines or in automated build logs; use -K - or variables from the environment.

quiz.q: How does a variable get substituted into a header?
quiz.explain: Expansion is opt-in per option through the --expand- prefix.

concepts.name: URL globbing and parallel transfers
concepts.summary: Fetch many URLs in one command with [1-100] and {a,b} patterns, name the outputs with #1, and run transfers at the same time with -Z.
concepts.why: Bulk downloads and quick load checks become one efficient command instead of a slow shell loop.
concepts.body:
curl expands **URL globs** itself: patterns in a URL that stand for many URLs. Quote them so your shell leaves them alone:

- Ranges: `[1-100]`, with leading zeros `[001-100]`, steps `[0-100:10]`, letters `[a-z]`.
- Lists: `{alpha,beta,gamma}`.
- Several patterns multiply: `{eu,us}/day[1-7]` is 14 URLs.

When saving, `#1`, `#2`... in the `-o` name stand for the current value of the first, second pattern: `-o 'page_#1.json'`. With `-O`, the names from the URLs are used.

By default curl fetches the URLs one after another, but it **reuses connections**. So even one at a time is much faster than a shell loop that starts a new curl, and sets up a new connection and TLS, for every URL.

`-Z` / `--parallel` runs transfers at the same time, up to 50 at once by default (`--parallel-max` changes that). With HTTP/2, a newer version of HTTP, several of them can even share one connection. The output order isn't predictable in parallel mode, so write each URL to its own file.

Use `-g` / `--globoff` when a URL really contains `[` `]` or `{` `}`, such as a numeric IPv6 address, which URLs write inside brackets.

Several plain URLs work too: `curl -O url1 -O url2`. Each URL needs its own `-o` or `-O`, or use `--remote-name-all` once. Combine with `--fail` and `--retry` for robust bulk jobs, and respect the site's **rate limit**: how many requests it allows you per second or minute.
concepts.code:
curl -sS -o 'page_#1.json' 'https://api.example.com/items?page=[1-5]'
ls page_*      # page_1.json ... page_5.json
curl -sS -o '#1_#2.csv' 'https://data.example.com/{eu,us}/day[1-7].csv'   # 14 files
curl -Z --parallel-max 10 -fsS --remote-name-all \
     https://dl.example.com/part[001-120].bin
curl -g 'http://[::1]:8080/health'          # globbing off: [::1] is an IPv6 address
curl -sS -w '%{url} %{http_code} %{time_total}\n' \
     -o /dev/null https://example.com/ -o /dev/null https://example.com/about
takeaways: [1-10], [a-z], {a,b} patterns; #1 in -o names the output
One curl reuses connections across URLs; -Z runs transfers at the same time
-g turns patterns off for URLs with brackets
pitfalls: Forgetting to quote a globbed URL, so the shell expands or rejects the brackets and braces.

quiz.q: Which output name pattern saves `.../{a,b}/[1-2].txt` as `a-1.txt`, `a-2.txt`, ...?
quiz.explain: #1 and #2 are replaced with the current values of the first and second pattern.

concepts.name: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and connection behaviour
concepts.summary: See how curl picks HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, force a version for testing, and understand connection reuse and Alt-Svc.
concepts.why: Differences between HTTP versions explain performance results, trouble with proxies (servers that relay your traffic) and bugs that appear on only one version.
concepts.body:
Three HTTP versions are in use. HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection. HTTP/2 carries many at once over one connection. HTTP/3 does the same over a different kind of connection.

For `https://` URLs, a curl built with HTTP/2 support offers it during the TLS handshake through **ALPN**, a field where client and server agree which protocol to speak next. If the server agrees, HTTP/2 is used; otherwise curl falls back to HTTP/1.1. `-w '%{http_version}'` reports what was actually used.

Forcing versions for testing:

- `--http1.1` turns HTTP/2 off, useful when a proxy or server misbehaves with HTTP/2 ("h2").
- `--http2-prior-knowledge` speaks HTTP/2 over plain `http://` straight away, without asking first ("h2c"). Some internal services expect this.
- `--http3` tries HTTP/3 and falls back to older versions if it fails; `--http3-only` doesn't fall back. Both need a curl built with HTTP/3 support (look for `HTTP3` in `curl -V`).

HTTP/3 runs over **QUIC**, a newer way to carry connections, with encryption built in. QUIC sends its data as **UDP** packets: **packets** are the small chunks all network data is split into, and UDP sends them without any built-in delivery guarantees, leaving that work to QUIC.

Browsers find out a server speaks HTTP/3 from the **Alt-Svc** response header ("also available over h3 on port 443"). curl can do the same: `--alt-svc cache.txt` stores those headers and uses HTTP/3 on later requests.

Within one curl command, connections are kept open and **reused** for later URLs to the same host. With HTTP/2, parallel transfers (`-Z`) are **multiplexed**: their pieces interleave as separate streams over one connection. `%{num_connects}` shows how many new connections were opened.

**Head-of-line blocking** is why HTTP/3 exists. HTTP/2 runs over **TCP**, which hands data over strictly in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream until it's sent again, like one slow shopper holding up a single checkout. QUIC keeps streams independent. Compare versions on a poor connection with `-w '%{time_total}'` to see it.
concepts.code:
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://www.google.com     # 2
curl -sS --http1.1 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://www.google.com   # 1.1
curl -V | grep -o 'HTTP3'                         # is HTTP/3 compiled in?
curl -sS --http3 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://cloudflare.com    # 3
curl -sS --http2-prior-knowledge http://localhost:50051/   # h2c, no TLS
curl -sSI https://cloudflare.com | grep -i alt-svc
# alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400
curl -sS -o /dev/null -o /dev/null -w '%{num_connects} ' \
     https://example.com/ https://example.com/about   # 1 0  (second reused)
takeaways: HTTPS picks HTTP/2 through ALPN; -w %{http_version} shows the result
--http1.1, --http2-prior-knowledge, --http3, --http3-only force a version
Connections are reused within one command; Alt-Svc advertises HTTP/3
pitfalls: Assuming --http3 works everywhere; the curl that comes with many Linux systems lacks HTTP/3 support.

quiz.q: How does curl discover that an HTTPS server supports HTTP/2?
options: Through ALPN during the TLS handshake
It tries HTTP/2 first and retries on error
quiz.explain: ALPN lets client and server agree on HTTP/2 (h2) as part of setting up TLS.

concepts.name: Tracing, proxies and name resolution
concepts.summary: Record exact bytes with --trace-ascii, send traffic through a proxy with -x or proxy variables, and pin down name lookup problems with -4/-6.
concepts.why: Company proxies, odd DNS setups and 'the server says my body is wrong' problems need byte-by-byte visibility.
concepts.body:
`-v` shows headers, but not bodies or exact bytes. For that:

- `--trace-ascii trace.txt` (or `-` for standard output) records everything sent and received, bodies included, as readable text. `--trace` gives a **hex dump** instead: every byte written as a two-digit code. `--trace-time` adds the time to each line.
- Trace files contain tokens, passwords and cookies; scrub them before sharing.

**Proxies.** A **proxy** is a server that sits between you and the internet and passes your requests on; many companies require one. `-x http://proxy.corp:3128` sends the request through it. `socks5h://` uses a **SOCKS** proxy, a simpler kind that just relays connections, and lets the proxy look up names.

curl also reads proxy settings from environment variables: `https_proxy`, `all_proxy`, and `http_proxy` in lowercase only. Uppercase `HTTP_PROXY` is ignored on purpose. Under **CGI**, an old way for web servers to run scripts, request headers become environment variables named `HTTP_...`, so an attacker's `Proxy:` header would show up as `HTTP_PROXY`. `no_proxy=localhost,.internal` lists hosts that skip the proxy, and `--noproxy '*'` turns proxies off for one command.

For HTTPS through an HTTP proxy, curl sends a `CONNECT` request asking the proxy to open a tunnel, then runs TLS through it end to end, so the proxy can't read the traffic. `-v` shows the CONNECT exchange and the proxy's answer.

**Name resolution** is turning a host name into an IP address. `-4` / `-6` force IPv4 or the newer IPv6, which isolates the classic "slow first request" caused by a broken IPv6 route. `--dns-servers` picks which DNS servers to ask (only in curl builds that use the c-ares library), and `--doh-url https://dns.example/dns-query` uses **DNS-over-HTTPS**: name lookups sent as HTTPS requests. `%{remote_ip}` in `-w` confirms where you actually connected.
concepts.code:
curl -sS --trace-ascii - --json '{"a":1}' https://api.example.com/echo | head -20
# => Send header, 154 bytes ...  => Send data, 7 bytes: {"a":1}
curl -sS -x http://proxy.corp:3128 https://example.com -o /dev/null -v 2>&1 | grep CONNECT
# > CONNECT example.com:443 HTTP/1.1
export https_proxy=http://proxy.corp:3128 no_proxy=localhost,.internal
curl -sS https://example.com -o /dev/null            # through the proxy
curl -sS http://wiki.internal/ -o /dev/null           # direct (listed in no_proxy)
curl -sS --noproxy '*' https://example.com -o /dev/null   # direct this time
curl -4 -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{remote_ip} %{time_connect}\n' https://example.com
curl -x socks5h://localhost:1080 http://grafana.internal:3000/   # names looked up by the proxy
takeaways: --trace-ascii shows full bodies and exact bytes
-x or https_proxy/http_proxy (lowercase) send traffic through a proxy; no_proxy skips it
-4/-6 and %{remote_ip} isolate name lookup and IP-version problems
pitfalls: Setting HTTP_PROXY in uppercase and wondering why curl ignores it for http:// URLs.

quiz.q: curl ignores your `HTTP_PROXY=...` setting for http:// URLs. Why?
options: curl does not support HTTP proxies
For http_proxy curl reads only the lowercase name, for security reasons
The variable must be named CURL_PROXY
quiz.explain: Under CGI, an incoming Proxy: request header becomes the HTTP_PROXY variable, so an attacker could set it; curl only honours lowercase http_proxy.

concepts.name: libcurl: curl as a library
concepts.summary: libcurl is the C library behind curl, with easy and multi interfaces, versions for most languages, and --libcurl to turn a command into code.
concepts.why: Knowing libcurl explains curl's behaviour and lets you move a working command into a program.
concepts.body:
The `curl` command is a thin layer over **libcurl**, a **library**: ready-made code that other programs build in and call. libcurl is written in the C language and runs in cars, TVs, game consoles, PHP, Python (pycurl), git's downloads and countless apps. Every command-line option maps to a library setting. The example below is in C; you can follow the steps without knowing C.

The **easy interface** handles one transfer, and your program waits until it's done (it is **synchronous**):

- `curl_easy_init()` creates a **handle**, an object holding the settings for one transfer.
- `curl_easy_setopt(h, CURLOPT_URL, ...)` and other `CURLOPT_*` options configure it.
- `curl_easy_perform(h)` runs the transfer and returns a `CURLcode`: the same numbers as the command's exit codes.
- `curl_easy_cleanup(h)` frees it. Reusing one handle for more requests keeps its connections open for reuse.

The **multi interface** drives many easy handles at the same time from a single **thread**, one line of execution in a program. It works as an **event loop**: one loop that keeps checking which transfers can move forward (`curl_multi_perform`, `curl_multi_poll`). That's how `curl -Z` works.

The fastest way to start: get the command working with the curl tool, then add `--libcurl code.c`. curl writes a C program that sets the matching options, which is also a great way to learn which `CURLOPT` matches a flag.

Library defaults differ from the command in places: libcurl doesn't follow redirects or read `.curlrc`. And a **callback**, a function of yours that libcurl calls when data arrives (set with `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION`), receives the data in pieces of any size, so never assume one call holds the whole response.
takeaways: Easy interface: init, setopt, perform, cleanup
The multi interface runs many transfers at once from one thread
--libcurl file.c turns a working command into C code
pitfalls: Assuming the write callback receives the whole response at once; it is called with pieces.

options: Performs the request and writes C code that does the same with libcurl
quiz.explain: --libcurl records the options used by the command as a libcurl program.
